title: How to Find the Age of a Furnace, Boiler or Water Heater
description: A practical guide for landlords to find how old the heating equipment and water heaters in each rental are, using labels, serial numbers, and paperwork.
body:
December is when heating equipment does its hardest work. Furnaces and boilers run for long stretches, and water heaters take in colder water and work harder to warm it. If one of them is near the end of its life, winter is a likely time for it to fail.

You can't plan for a replacement if you don't know how old the equipment is. Many small landlords inherited their systems from a previous owner and never checked. The good news is that age is usually findable in a few minutes per unit, without a technician.

Here is how to do it, and what to write down once you know.

## Start with the data plate

Every furnace, boiler, water heater and outdoor AC unit has a rating plate or sticker from the manufacturer. That is your best source.

Where to find it:

- **Gas or electric water heaters:** usually a large sticker on the side of the tank, often near the gas valve or the upper element cover.
- **Furnaces:** inside the front panel, on the blower compartment door or the cabinet wall. Turn off power at the service switch before removing a panel.
- **Boilers:** on the side or front of the jacket, sometimes behind a removable cover.
- **Outdoor AC or heat pump units:** on the side of the cabinet, often near the electrical connections.

Take a clear photo of the whole plate before you try to read it. A phone flashlight held at an angle helps with faded print. The photo also gives you a permanent record, so you don't have to go back into the unit later.

Some plates list a manufacture date in plain words. If yours does, you're done. If not, the serial number is the next step.

## How to read the serial number

Most manufacturers encode the month and year of manufacture inside the serial number. The trouble is that each brand does it differently, and some brands have changed their format over the years.

Common patterns you'll see:

- **Four digits for week or month and year**, such as a section that reads like a two-digit month followed by a two-digit year.
- **A letter for the month**, where A stands for January, B for February, and so on, paired with digits for the year.
- **Letter codes on a repeating cycle**, where the same letter can mean years that are decades apart. For these you need the brand's own chart and some common sense about which decade fits.

The reliable way to decode it:

1. Write down the brand, model number and full serial number from your photo.
2. Search for the brand name plus "serial number date code." Many manufacturers publish their own decoder or chart.
3. If you can't find an official chart, call the manufacturer's customer support line with the model and serial. They can usually tell you the build date.
4. Sanity check the result. A water heater that decodes to a date before the building's last major renovation might be original, or it might mean you read the code wrong.

Keep in mind that manufacture date and install date are not the same. Equipment can sit in a warehouse for a while before it goes in. For planning, the manufacture date is close enough and errs slightly on the cautious side.

## When the label is missing or unreadable

Older equipment often has a peeled, rusted or painted-over plate. You still have options:

- **Installer stickers.** Plumbers and HVAC contractors often put their own sticker on the unit with an install date or service history.
- **Permit records.** Many cities and counties require permits for water heater and furnace replacements. Your local building department may be able to look up permits by address.
- **Closing documents.** Your purchase inspection report frequently notes the approximate age of major systems. Check your files from when you bought the building.
- **Previous owner or property manager.** A quick email can turn up old invoices.
- **Refrigerant type on AC units.** Outdoor units built to use R-22 refrigerant are generally from before the 2010 phase-out of R-22 in new equipment. That doesn't give you an exact year, but it tells you the unit is old.
- **Your next service visit.** If a technician is already coming out, ask them to estimate the age and note it on the invoice.

If all else fails, make a reasonable estimate and label it as an estimate. A rough age you can plan around is far more useful than a blank cell.

## What to record for each system

Once you have ages, put them somewhere you'll actually look again. For each piece of equipment, record:

- Building and unit
- System type (water heater, furnace, boiler, AC, heat pump)
- Brand, model and serial number
- Fuel type and size (for example, a 40-gallon gas tank)
- Manufacture or install year, and whether it's confirmed or estimated
- Source of the date (plate, permit, invoice, inspection report)
- Last service date and any known issues
- Photo of the data plate

If you're starting from scratch, our free [CapEx spreadsheet template](/capex-spreadsheet-template) has columns for all of this. Recording the source matters more than it seems. When a number looks off in two years, you'll know whether to trust it.

## Turn ages into a replacement plan

Age on its own is just a number. It becomes useful when you compare it against a typical lifespan for that type of equipment and see which items are coming due.

A simple way to sort what you found:

1. **Past typical lifespan:** expect replacement soon. Get a quote now so you aren't shopping in an emergency.
2. **Within a few years of typical lifespan:** start setting money aside specifically for these.
3. **Mid-life or newer:** keep up with routine maintenance and check again next year.

Water heaters in multiple units often share a similar age if they were installed during the same renovation. That can mean several replacements land close together, which is worth knowing before it happens.

You can check typical ranges for each system on our [lifespan reference](/lifespan). If you'd rather not do the math by hand, CapexClock takes the ages you've gathered and lays out a 10-year replacement forecast for each building, along with the reserve amount that schedule implies.

Whichever way you track it, a short walk-through this month with a phone camera can save you from finding out a boiler's age the hard way in January.

title: How long do roofs, HVAC and water heaters last in a rental?
description: Typical lifespans for the big-ticket systems in a rental property, why your building may not match the average, and how to use the numbers to plan replacements.
body:
Every rental has a handful of systems that will need replacing someday: the roof, the furnace and AC, the water heaters, the appliances, the flooring. The hard part isn't knowing that they'll wear out. It's knowing roughly *when*, so the cost doesn't land as a surprise.

Here are typical lifespans for the systems that matter most, and how to use them.

## Typical lifespans

These are common ranges, in years. Your building may land outside them, and the next section explains why.

### Roofing

- **Asphalt shingle roof:** about 20 to 25
- **Flat or membrane roof:** about 15 to 25
- **Gutters and downspouts:** about 20 to 30

### Heating and cooling

- **Gas furnace:** about 15 to 20
- **Central AC or condenser:** about 12 to 15
- **Heat pump:** about 12 to 15
- **Boiler:** about 20 to 30

### Plumbing

- **Tank water heater:** about 8 to 12
- **Tankless water heater:** about 15 to 20

### Appliances

- **Refrigerator:** about 10 to 15
- **Range or oven:** about 13 to 15
- **Dishwasher:** about 9 to 12
- **Washer and dryer:** about 10 to 13

### Floors and finishes

- **Carpet:** about 5 to 10
- **Luxury vinyl plank:** about 15 to 25
- **Interior paint:** about 3 to 7, often at turnover

The [component lifespan chart](/lifespan) has these and more, with a page for each system.

## Why your building may not match

A lifespan range is an average across a lot of buildings. Yours is one building. A few things push it one way or the other:

- **Climate.** Hot summers are hard on AC units and roofs. Long winters work furnaces harder.
- **Water quality.** Hard water shortens the life of water heaters and dishwashers.
- **Install quality.** A well-installed system with proper venting and drainage tends to outlast a rushed one.
- **Maintenance.** Changing filters, flushing water heaters and clearing gutters really does add years.
- **Tenant turnover.** Frequent move-outs are hard on carpet, paint and appliances.

So treat the range as a starting point, not a promise. If your water heater is 10 years old and the area has hard water, plan as if it's near the end, even though 10 is inside the range.

## How to find the age of what you have

You can't plan without knowing how old things are. A few places to look:

- **Labels and serial numbers.** Most water heaters, furnaces and AC units have a manufacture date printed on the label or encoded in the serial number.
- **Closing documents and inspection reports.** These often list the age or condition of major systems.
- **Receipts and permits.** If a system was replaced, the invoice or permit has the date.
- **Your best estimate.** If none of that exists, an honest guess is better than a blank. You can update it later.

## Turning lifespans into a plan

Once you have an age and a typical lifespan for each system, you can see roughly when each one will come due. Put them on a timeline and two things usually stand out:

1. **Something is closer than you thought.** Often a water heater or an AC unit that's quietly near the end.
2. **Several things line up in the same few years.** Systems installed together tend to wear out together, which can make for one very expensive stretch.

Seeing that ahead of time is the whole point. It gives you years, not days, to set money aside.

If you'd like help with that step, the free [CapEx calculator](/capex-calculator) takes each system's age and cost and lays out a 10-year replacement forecast with a monthly reserve number.

## Keep it current

Lifespans don't change much, but your building does. When you replace something, update its install date. When you get a new quote, update the cost. A once-a-year check keeps the plan honest without much work.

title: How much should you set aside for CapEx on a rental property?
description: Rules of thumb like 5% or 10% of rent are a start, but your roof and HVAC don't know your rent. Here's how to work out a CapEx number from your actual building.
body:
Ask ten landlords how much to set aside for capital expenditures and you'll hear "5% of rent," "10% of rent," "$100 a door," and "whatever's left." All of them can be right for someone. None of them is based on the thing that actually breaks: your building.

This post walks through why the rules of thumb drift, and how to get a monthly CapEx number from the systems you actually own.

## What counts as CapEx

Capital expenditures are the big, occasional replacements that keep a property working: roof, HVAC, water heater, appliances, flooring, windows, siding, paving. They're different from repairs (fixing a leak, replacing a faucet), which come up all the time and usually belong in your maintenance budget.

The problem with CapEx isn't that it's unpredictable. You know a roof will need replacing. The problem is that it arrives in large, lumpy amounts, often years apart, and it's easy to spend the money in between.

## Why percentage-of-rent rules drift

A percentage of rent is easy to use, and for a lot of small portfolios it's a reasonable first guess. But rent and replacement cost aren't connected:

- **Two houses with the same rent can have very different CapEx.** A 1960s house with an old roof and original windows needs far more than a five-year-old build renting for the same amount.
- **Age matters more than rent.** A 15-year-old furnace is closer to the end of its life than a 3-year-old one, whatever the tenant pays.
- **Costs rise faster in some places than rents do.** A percentage set years ago may no longer cover the jobs it was meant for.

So a percentage can leave you over-saving on a newer property and badly under-saving on an older one.

## A better way: one line per system

Instead of starting from rent, start from the building. For each big system, you need three numbers:

1. **What it costs to replace.** A recent quote or invoice is best. A typical range is fine to start.
2. **How long it lasts.** Most components have a typical lifespan. A tank water heater might last around 8 to 12 years, an asphalt shingle roof around 20 to 30. See the [component lifespan chart](/lifespan) for common ranges.
3. **How old yours is.** The install date, or your best guess from an inspection report.

From those, the monthly amount for one system is roughly:

> Replacement cost ÷ months until it's due

### A worked example

Say a duplex has a water heater that cost $1,800 to replace, is expected to last 10 years, and is 6 years old. It's due in about 4 years, or 48 months.

> $1,800 ÷ 48 months ≈ $38 a month

Now do the same for the roof, the furnace, the AC, the appliances and the flooring, and add the lines up. That total is your building's CapEx number, based on what's actually there.

The example numbers are just examples. Use your own costs, because local prices vary a lot.

## Three things that trip people up

**Systems that are already overdue.** If a component is past its typical life, there are no months left to spread the cost over. Treat it as a near-term expense, and keep some cash ready, rather than pretending it will last another decade.

**Everything coming due at once.** Systems installed in the same year tend to wear out in the same few years. A building where the roof, HVAC and water heater were all replaced in 2012 can face a very expensive stretch around the same time. Lay your replacements out on a timeline so you can see the busy years coming.

**Forgetting the small big things.** Appliances, flooring and paint turnovers don't feel like CapEx, but across several units they add up. Give them a line too.

## How to keep it simple

You don't need a perfect model. A list of your major systems with a cost, a lifespan and an age gets you most of the way. Revisit it once a year, update anything you replaced, and adjust costs when you get new quotes.

If you'd like a head start, the free [CapEx calculator](/capex-calculator) turns that list into a 10-year replacement forecast and one monthly reserve number, and the [reserve calculator](/reserve-calculator) gives a quick estimate if you only have a few minutes.

## The short answer

How much should you set aside? Enough to cover each system's replacement by the time it's due. Percentage rules are a fine place to start, but the number that will actually protect you comes from your own roof, HVAC and water heaters.

title: Repair or Replace an Old Furnace or Boiler in a Rental?
description: A calm, step-by-step way to decide whether to repair or replace an aging furnace or boiler in a rental, especially when it fails in the middle of winter.
body:
It's December, the heating season is in full swing, and a tenant calls to say the heat is out. The technician fixes it, or quotes a repair, and then says the line every landlord eventually hears: "Honestly, this unit is getting old. You might want to think about replacing it."

Now you have to decide, often fast and often with a cold tenant waiting. This post walks through a simple way to make the repair-or-replace call on a furnace or boiler in a rental, and how to set things up so the next decision is less rushed.

## Start with three facts

Before any rule of thumb, get three pieces of information written down. Most bad decisions come from deciding without them.

1. **The age of the equipment.** Check the data plate for a manufacture date or decode the serial number. If you're not sure how, we have a separate guide on finding the age of a furnace, boiler or water heater.
2. **The repair quote, in writing.** Ask what failed, what the repair includes, and whether the technician expects other parts to fail soon.
3. **The repair history.** How many service calls in the last two or three years? A unit that has needed one repair in a decade is different from one that needs a visit every winter.

With those three facts, you can compare the system's age to its typical lifespan. You can look up typical ranges for furnaces and boilers at /lifespan. Boilers often outlast furnaces, but the range for both is wide and depends on maintenance, water quality and how hard the system works.

## Rules of thumb, and where they break

You'll hear a few common shortcuts from contractors and other owners:

- **The 50% rule.** If the repair costs more than about half of a replacement, lean toward replacing.
- **The age-times-cost rule.** Multiply the system's age by the repair cost. If the result is above a set threshold, replace. Different contractors use different thresholds, so treat it loosely.
- **The end-of-life rule.** If the unit is already past its typical lifespan, a major repair is usually money spent on borrowed time.

These are useful starting points, not answers. They break down in a few situations:

- **Cheap repair, old unit.** A small part on a very old furnace is often worth fixing to get through the winter, as long as you start planning the replacement now.
- **Expensive repair, young unit.** A big repair on a system with years of life left is usually worth doing, especially if parts or labor are under warranty.
- **Safety issues.** A cracked heat exchanger, venting problems or carbon monoxide concerns change the conversation entirely. Follow the technician's safety guidance first and run the numbers second.

## Rental-specific factors homeowners don't have to weigh

A furnace in your own house and a furnace in a rental are different decisions. A few things to factor in:

**Heat is usually a legal requirement.** Many cities and states set minimum indoor temperatures and response times for heat outages. A repair that restores heat today may matter more than the perfect long-term choice next week.

**Who pays the utilities.** If tenants pay for heat, efficiency gains mostly help them, which can still help with retention and vacancy. If you pay for heat, for example with a central boiler, a more efficient system shows up directly in your operating costs.

**Units installed at the same time.** In small multifamily buildings, furnaces or water heaters were often all installed in the same year. If one is failing from age, the others are probably close behind. That's worth knowing before you decide, because one replacement may really be the first of several.

**Timing and contractor availability.** Mid-winter replacements can mean longer waits and less room to compare quotes. If an old unit can be repaired safely now, you may get better options by planning a replacement for spring or early fall.

**Turnover.** If a unit is about to turn over, replacing equipment while it's vacant is usually simpler than working around a tenant.

## A simple decision walkthrough

When the call comes in, try working through these questions in order:

1. **Is it safe?** If the technician flags a safety issue, act on that first.
2. **Can heat be restored quickly?** If yes, that buys you time to decide calmly.
3. **Where is the unit in its lifespan?** Early, middle, or near or past the end?
4. **How does the repair compare to replacement?** Get a rough replacement quote even if you plan to repair.
5. **Is this a pattern?** Repeated calls on the same unit point toward replacement.
6. **Are other units the same age?** If so, plan for the group, not just this one.
7. **Can you fund the replacement now?** If not, a repair plus a dated plan is often the practical answer.

Write down what you decided and why. Next winter, you'll be glad you did.

## If you repair, plan the replacement anyway

Choosing to repair an aging system isn't a mistake. It's often the right call. The mistake is repairing and then forgetting about it until the next failure, usually on a cold night.

After any significant repair on an older furnace or boiler:

- **Record the date, the repair, and the cost** next to the unit's age.
- **Pick a target replacement year**, based on its age and typical lifespan.
- **Start setting money aside for it.** Divide the expected replacement cost by the months until your target date. That gives you a concrete monthly amount instead of a vague worry.
- **Repeat for the other big systems** in the building: roofs, water heaters and the rest of the HVAC.

If you'd like a starting point, the free template at /capex-spreadsheet-template lays these items out by building, and /reserve-calculator turns replacement dates and costs into a monthly reserve figure. CapexClock does the same thing across your roofs, HVAC and water heaters, turning install years into a 10-year replacement forecast and a monthly per-unit reserve number, so the next failing boiler is a line you already saw coming.

The heating season will always produce some surprise calls. The goal isn't to prevent every one. It's to make sure that when the technician says "you might want to replace this," you already know roughly when, roughly how much, and where the money is coming from.

title: A year-end checklist for small rental property owners
description: December is a good time to look back at your rentals and plan ahead. A short checklist covering replacements, reserves, records and what's coming due next year.
body:
The end of the year is a natural moment to step back from day-to-day landlording and look at the bigger picture. You have a full year of repairs, replacements and receipts to learn from, and a new year to plan for.

Here's a checklist you can work through in an afternoon. It's written for owners with a handful of units up to a few dozen, but most of it applies at any size.

## 1. List what you replaced this year

Go through the year and write down every major replacement: a roof, a furnace, a water heater, appliances, flooring.

For each one, note:

- **What it was** and which property or unit.
- **When** it was replaced.
- **What it cost**, all in, including labor and disposal.

This list does two things. It updates your records with new install dates, which resets the clock on those systems. And it gives you real local costs to plan with next time, which are much better than national averages.

## 2. Update ages and conditions

For anything you didn't replace, add a year to its age. Then take a quick look at the big systems if you can:

- Any signs the roof is aging, like curling shingles or granules in the gutters?
- Did the AC struggle this summer, or the furnace this winter?
- Any water heaters showing rust or small leaks?

Condition notes help you decide which systems might come due early.

## 3. See what's due next year

With updated ages, look at which systems are at or near the end of their typical lifespan. The [component lifespan chart](/lifespan) has common ranges if you need them.

Make a short list of what's likely in the next 12 months and roughly what each would cost. This is the list that should drive your reserve planning, not a percentage of rent.

## 4. Check your reserves

Compare what you have set aside for capital expenses with what's coming due:

- **Is the balance enough** to cover next year's likely replacements?
- **Did you spend more than you saved** this year? If so, why?
- **Is a big year coming** in the next three to five years, when several systems line up?

If the numbers don't line up, now is the time to adjust your monthly set-aside. A small increase starting in January is much easier than a scramble in July. The [reserve calculator](/reserve-calculator) gives a quick estimate if you want a starting point.

## 5. Gather your records

Pull together the paperwork you'll need for taxes and for your own planning:

- Receipts and invoices for repairs and replacements.
- Rent rolls and income for each property.
- Insurance policies and any claims.
- Contracts with vendors and property managers.

Keep replacements separate from ordinary repairs. Your tax preparer will want to know which is which, and the difference matters for your own planning too.

## 6. Plan the work you can schedule

Some replacements don't have to wait for a failure. If a system is clearly near the end, replacing it on your own schedule is usually cheaper and less disruptive than an emergency call.

- **Book off-season work early.** AC work is easier to schedule in the spring, roofing in drier months, furnace work before the cold.
- **Time it with turnover.** Flooring, paint and appliances are easiest to replace between tenants.
- **Get quotes now** for anything big you expect next year.

## 7. Write down one lesson

Finish with one sentence about what you'd do differently. Maybe it's "start tracking water heater ages," "raise the monthly reserve," or "get two quotes for anything over a set amount." One lesson a year adds up.

## Keep it simple

None of this needs special software. A spreadsheet with one row per system, its age, its expected life and its replacement cost gets you most of the way. If you'd like a head start, there's a free [CapEx spreadsheet template](/capex-spreadsheet-template) you can download and fill in.
